name: Independent on Sunday cryptic crossword No 1,379

clue.text: Climber saw Everest regularly when travelling around central Nepal

indicators.note: regularly means taking letters at even intervals, here every other one of the mountain's name
something travelling is on the move, so the letters move about into a new order
around means the shuffled letters go round the outside of the next piece
central picks out the single middle letter of the country's name

blocks.note: taken as written
the first, third, fifth and seventh letters
the middle letter of a five-letter word

explanation.surface: A mountaineer tackles Everest on an expedition through the heart of Nepal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' points at a mountaineer, but it is a climbing plant. The shuffled letters split around the Nepal letter rather than sitting in one block.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet pea is a garden plant that scrambles upwards using tendrils, so it is a climbing plant.

clue.text: In what respect is her wine fruity?

indicators.note: a fruity wine is rich and lively, suggesting the letters are mixed up into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A wine taster asks in what way her wine counts as fruity.
explanation.definitionFit: Wherein is a formal word asking or stating in which way or in which matter something holds.

clue.text: Initially moving to the end, let's stand

indicators.note: the word's opening letter is taken from the front and put at the back

blocks.note: to let property is to lease it, so 'let's' stands for lease

explanation.surface: Someone suggests a move to the end of a queue and a wait standing up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let's' reads as 'let us', but here it is 'let' in the sense of renting out. Moving LEASE's first letter to the back gives EASEL.
explanation.definitionFit: An easel is a wooden frame on legs that holds an artist's canvas upright: a stand.

clue.text: Priest, at one with God, is leader by example, perhaps

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for priest
an ace is a one in cards and dice
the Maker is a name for God as creator

explanation.surface: A priest at one with his God sets a moral example to others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at one with God' sounds like spiritual harmony; 'one' is the card and 'God' the Creator.
explanation.definitionFit: A pacemaker in a race leads the field and sets the speed for others to follow, leading by example.

clue.text: Chilling in Rio, I relaxed with gin and tonic

indicators.note: relaxed means loosened up, so the letters are loosened and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker chills out in Rio with a gin and tonic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chilling' looks like taking it easy, but it means cooling air. 'With' joins the fodder pieces: 'Rio, I', 'and', 'gin' and 'tonic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Air-conditioning is the system that cools the air in a building or car, literally a chilling process.

clue.text: Newspaper cutting includes brief summary

indicators.note: includes says the letters sit inside the run of words before it

blocks.note: found spanning the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A press clipping contains a short summary of the story.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits after the indicator, so 'Newspaper cutting' is purely the container of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperçu, borrowed from French, is a brief outline or quick insight into a subject.

clue.text: It's comparatively straight, Uncle's side parting

indicators.note: one side of a word is an end of it, here the opening letter

blocks.note: from the idiom 'as straight as a die': a die is the thing used for comparison
the letter at one end of the word

explanation.surface: A tidy hair parting on one side of an uncle's head.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'straight as a die' is the comparison: A DIE is what something is compared with to call it straight.
explanation.definitionFit: Adieu is the French farewell, used in English for a goodbye at a parting of ways.

clue.text: Mr Long rebuilt extension at the front - that's radical

indicators.note: here long means written out in full, giving the form a title takes before it is shortened
rebuilt means put together again differently, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: EXT is the usual abbreviation for an extension, placed first
the title written out in full

explanation.surface: A Mr Long has built an unusual front extension on his house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mr Long' reads as a man's name; it means the abbreviation Mr written long, as MISTER.
explanation.definitionFit: An extremist holds radical views far from the mainstream, so the noun matches radical used of a person.

clue.text: What might you have after being distressed? Tea?

definitions.text: What might you have after being distressed? Tea?

blocks.clueFragment: What might you have after being distressed? Tea?
blocks.note: surface reading: after an upset, the comforting thing to have is a cup of tea
setter's reading: dis-tressed, with your tresses (long hair) removed, leaving a very short haircut

explanation.walkthrough: The answer comes from reading 'distressed' as having lost your tresses; the closing 'Tea?' is a decoy pointing at the remedy for real distress.
explanation.definitionFit: A crew cut is a very short, close-cropped hairstyle, exactly what remains once long hair is shorn away.

clue.text: One growls - he's nervous, biting Camilla at first?

definitions.text: One growls - he's nervous, biting Camilla at first?

indicators.note: nervous means jittery and unsettled, so these letters are jumbled
at first takes just the opening letter of the name
biting means the jumbled letters close around the next piece like jaws

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written
taken as written
the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: A snarling royal pet, nervous of the Queen consort, sinks its teeth into Camilla.
explanation.walkthrough: 'he's nervous' reads as 'he is nervous': the 's is a link. The whole clue also describes the dog: Camilla is the royal consort, and the royal family's corgis were famous snappers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh corgi is a short-legged dog breed, kept by the British royal family, that can certainly growl and bite.

clue.text: Little time to start 15 Across

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
wee is a Scottish word for small

explanation.surface: A small moment of time is all it takes to start something delicate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to start' puts the time letter at the front, ahead of the word for little. 15 Across is DAINTY.
explanation.definitionFit: Twee describes something excessively quaint or cute, a sense close to dainty used of delicate prettiness.

clue.text: Jacket needed for voyage - consider sheepskin?

indicators.note: a jacket is the outer covering, so only the outside letters of the next word are kept

blocks.note: the first and last letters
to mull something over is to consider it

explanation.surface: A traveller ponders whether a sheepskin jacket is needed for the voyage.
explanation.walkthrough: No word in the clue signals that the word for consider is turned round. The question mark admits vellum is properly calfskin rather than sheepskin.
explanation.definitionFit: Vellum is fine parchment made from animal skin, usually calf, so sheepskin is an example with a hedging question mark.

clue.text: Old coppers having seized most of haul retired in luxury

indicators.note: most of means all but the last letter is kept
retired means drawn back, so the shortened word is read backwards
having seized means the coins word grabs the next piece and holds it inside

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
coppers are low-value coins, pennies
to lug is to haul something heavy

explanation.surface: Retired police officers who seized most of a criminal haul now live in luxury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old coppers' suggests ex-policemen; coppers are pennies, and 'Old' is just O.
explanation.definitionFit: Opulence means great wealth and lavish display, a close synonym for luxury.

clue.text: Removed stitching from uniform and cut around edge of pocket

indicators.note: the edge of a word is its first letter
around means the word for cut goes round the outside of the selected letter

blocks.note: U is uniform in the NATO alphabet
nicked means made a small cut in
the opening letter

explanation.surface: A tailor alters a uniform, unpicking it and trimming round the pocket edge.
explanation.definitionFit: To unpick a garment is to take out its stitching thread by thread, so unpicked means removed the stitches.

clue.text: Nurse and soldier give support to popular public official

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting means sitting underneath, so those parts follow the word for popular

blocks.note: in means fashionable, popular
to nurse is to tend
a soldier ant is a kind of ant, so soldier stands for ant

explanation.surface: A nurse and a soldier back a well-liked local official.
explanation.definitionFit: An intendant is a historical administrator or superintendent, especially in France or Spain, a public official.

clue.text: Daughter is not, in conclusion, very elegant

indicators.note: in conclusion points to the last letter of the word

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter
ain't is the colloquial contraction of is not
the final letter

explanation.surface: A father admits his daughter is not, in the end, very elegant.
explanation.definitionFit: Dainty describes something delicately pretty and graceful, close in sense to elegant.

clue.text: Anger for one in England's tail; delays unsettled batting

indicators.note: a word's tail is its final letter
unsettled means disturbed from its order, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the final letter
taken as written
in cricket a side batting is in

explanation.surface: Fans fume at England's tail-end batsmen, whose delays leave the innings unsettled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'England's tail' suggests the lower-order batsmen in cricket, but it is the last letter of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Anger, or wrath, is one of the seven deadly sins of Christian teaching, so it is an example.

clue.text: Curry was a good one - odd bits of tikka cooked in spice, extremely rich, served for starters

indicators.note: odd bits are the first, third and fifth letters
cooked means prepared and changed, so those letters are rearranged
in means the shuffled letters go inside the next piece
extremely keeps only the two end letters of the word
for starters takes the opening letter

blocks.note: the first and last letters
letters one, three and five
the opening letter

explanation.surface: A restaurant review: the curry was good, a tikka in rich spice with starters.
explanation.walkthrough: Curry looks like the food but is John Curry, the British figure skater who won Olympic gold in 1976.
explanation.definitionFit: John Curry was an Olympic champion figure skater, so he was a good skater, a person defined by example.

clue.text: One belittles attention-seeker

blocks.note: first meaning: someone who knocks, or runs down, others
second meaning: the metal device on a front door used to get the household's attention

explanation.surface: Someone who puts others down is just after attention.
explanation.definitionFit: A knocker is both a critic who disparages and the hinged fitting a visitor bangs to summon someone to the door.

clue.text: Ultimately smitten with old Italian car, beginning to think about purchase ...

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the next word
beginning to takes the opening letter of the word that follows
about means moved around, so all the collected letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the final letter
O is the abbreviation for old
IT is the abbreviation for Italian
taken as written
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Smitten with a classic Italian car, someone starts to consider buying it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'purchase' suggests buying the car, but it means grip. The ellipsis just runs the story into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Purchase can mean a firm hold or grip, and traction is the grip of a tyre or wheel on a surface.

clue.text: Coffee being splattered over front of newspaper shows discourtesy

indicators.note: something splattered is splashed about, so these letters are scattered into a new order
the front of a word is its first letter
over means the scrambled letters cover the selected letter, lying round it

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Spilling coffee over someone's morning paper is rude.
explanation.definitionFit: Giving offence is causing hurt through rudeness, so offence here means an act of discourtesy or insult.

clue.text: ... grabbing key to new Ford Transit, it's how you might travel when commuting

definitions.text: how you might travel when commuting

indicators.note: grabbing means the following words take hold of the key letter and hold it inside
a thing in transit is moving, so the car maker's letters shift places

blocks.note: taken as written
A is a musical key
N is the abbreviation for new
taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing the story: grabbing the keys to a new Ford Transit van for the daily commute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ford Transit' is a well-known van, but Transit is the anagram signal for Ford. TO and N take A inside before the shuffled Ford follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Going to and fro means travelling back and forth, as a commuter does daily between home and work.

clue.text: Was angry having mishandled black-out?

indicators.note: out means the colour's abbreviation is taken away from the longer word

blocks.note: to fumble is to handle clumsily
BL is a standard abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: Someone seethed after a power cut was handled badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'black-out' looks like a power cut; it splits as 'black' plus the instruction 'out'.
explanation.definitionFit: To fume is to seethe with anger, so fumed is the past tense meaning was angry.

clue.text: Song's out of tune - stop!

blocks.note: a lay is a song or ballad
off-key, not right

explanation.surface: Someone cries out to a singer whose song is off-key: stop!
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in 'Song's' stands for 'is', joining the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay off is an informal command to quit doing something, so it can replace the imperative stop.

clue.text: Former employment program used to maintain old city dwellings

indicators.note: to maintain is to hold up, so the scheme's letters hold the city within

blocks.note: the Youth Training Scheme, a 1980s British government job-training programme
Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city

explanation.surface: An old jobs scheme was once used to keep up an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: YTS, the Youth Training Scheme, was a British programme for school leavers in the 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: Yurts are circular felt tents used as homes by nomads in Central Asia, so they are dwellings.

clue.text: Plant has fine strand in the centre

indicators.note: in the centre keeps only the middle pair of letters

blocks.note: OK means fine, all right
the two middle letters of a six-letter word

explanation.surface: A plant has a fine fibre running through its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Okra is a flowering plant grown for its edible green pods, also called ladies' fingers.

clue.text: Watch driver have prang - I'm worried about insurance

indicators.note: worried means agitated, so these letters are shaken into a new order
about means the shuffled letters go round the next abbreviation

blocks.note: taken as written; a prang is a British slang word for a minor car crash
INS is the abbreviation for insurance

explanation.surface: A motorist has had a minor crash and frets about the insurance claim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch driver' reads as a warning to a motorist, but it means the part that drives a watch.
explanation.definitionFit: The mainspring is the coiled spring that powers a mechanical clock or watch, so it drives the movement.

clue.text: Good value Dutch cheese, processed thus

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
to value something is to rate it
D is the abbreviation for Dutch

explanation.surface: A shopper finds good-value Dutch cheese, sold ready-processed.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reaches back to 'cheese': the answer describes cheese treated this way. 'Dutch cheese' looks like one phrase, but Dutch is only D.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheese is often shredded on a grater before cooking, so grated describes cheese processed that way.

clue.text: In short, one of the Krays, going around harbouring uneasiness?

definitions.text: In short, one of the Krays, going around harbouring uneasiness?

indicators.note: in short means using the shortened form of a twin's first name before it is turned
going around means turning back on itself, so the name is read right to left
harbouring means sheltering something inside, so the reversed name holds the next word

blocks.note: Reggie Kray, shortened to Reg
angst is anxiety, a feeling of unease

explanation.surface: One of the Kray twins walks about looking anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: Ronnie and Reggie Kray were twin gangsters who ruled London's East End in the 1960s, so the whole clue also defines the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Krays ran an organised criminal gang through violence and racketeering, which makes each of them a gangster.
